common_name: Blue Hill Salvia (Blauhugel Sky-Blue Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Blue Hill is distinguished from other meadow sage cultivars by its true, clear sky-blue flower color rather than the violet-blue or purple-blue tones common in the group.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean garden soil in full sun, spacing plants so the upright clumps can fill in without crowding. Blue Hill sends up dense, slender spikes of small, clear sky-blue flowers over aromatic, wrinkled gray-green foliage in late spring to early summer, and shearing the spent spikes back by about half typically brings on a second, lighter flush later in the season. The clear blue color reads differently in the border than the more common violet-blue meadow sage cultivars, making it a useful companion for pink, yellow, or white-flowered neighbors, and the tubular flowers are readily visited by bees and occasional hummingbirds throughout the bloom period.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Marcus Salvia (Dwarf Compact Violet-Blue Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Marcus is one of the most compact meadow sage cultivars available, forming a tidy, dense mound well suited to border edges and containers where taller salvias would flop or overwhelm the space.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, giving each plant enough room to form its own dense, rounded mound. Marcus produces a profusion of short, tightly packed violet-blue flower spikes held just above the compact foliage from late spring into summer, and its small stature keeps the whole plant self-supporting without staking even after rain. Shearing off spent spikes encourages continued flowering and keeps the mound neat through the season. Its long bloom period and dense flower production make it a reliable, low-maintenance nectar source for bees and small butterflies at the front of a sunny bed or in mixed containers.

common_name: Rose Marvel Salvia (Rose-Pink Compact Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Rose Marvel offers a rose-pink flower color that is uncommon among meadow sage cultivars, most of which run to blue, violet, or purple tones.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, and avoid heavy, wet clay where the crown can rot over winter. Rose Marvel forms a compact clump of upright spikes packed with small rose-pink flowers from late spring into summer, offering a warm-toned alternative to the blue and violet shades typical of the species, and it pairs well with silver-foliaged companions like artemisia or lamb's ear. Cutting back the first flush of spent flower stalks encourages a repeat bloom later in the season. Bees work the flower spikes steadily through the bloom period, and the compact habit suits the front to middle of a sunny perennial border.

common_name: Skyscraper Pink Salvia (Tall Well-Branched Pink Pollinator Salvia)

planting.note: Plant purchased transplants after the last frost into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Skyscraper Pink is a tall, tender perennial salvia grown as a warm-season annual outside its hardiness range, valued for its sturdy, self-branching, non-flopping habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, spacing plants to allow the tall, upright stems to branch freely without crowding. Skyscraper Pink produces long spikes of clear pink tubular flowers held well above the foliage on strong, sturdy stems that resist flopping even in wind or rain, making it a good choice for the back of a border or a bold vertical accent in a large container. The extended bloom period from summer through frost, combined with the large tubular flower shape, makes it especially attractive to hummingbirds. It behaves as a tender perennial in zones 8-10, sometimes resprouting from the roots after a mild winter, and is grown as a warm-season annual farther north; pinching young plants once encourages a fuller, more floriferous base.

common_name: Kudos Coral Agastache (Compact Coral-Pink Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Kudos Coral is part of a compact, heavy-flowering agastache series bred for garden performance and improved winter survival compared to older hummingbird mint selections.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage is the single most important factor for overwintering success, since agastache crowns are prone to rot in wet, heavy soils. Kudos Coral forms a dense, compact mound topped with tightly packed spikes of coral-pink flowers over aromatic, anise-scented foliage from early summer well into fall. The long, continuous bloom season and rich nectar make it a strong draw for bumble bees, honey bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies, and the compact habit keeps it tidy and self-supporting without staking. Leaving the seed heads standing through winter provides additional interest and food for finches.

common_name: Blue Boa Agastache (Large-Flowered Deep Violet-Blue Hyssop)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Blue Boa was bred for unusually large flower spikes and a deeper violet-blue color than most garden agastache hybrids.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, and avoid low spots where water collects over winter. Blue Boa produces unusually large, dense spikes of deep violet-blue flowers over aromatic, mint-scented foliage from midsummer through fall, giving it more visual weight in the border than many finer-textured agastache cultivars. The abundant nectar-rich flowers draw hummingbirds, bumble bees, and butterflies steadily through the long bloom season, and the sturdy upright stems hold up well without staking. Once established it tolerates heat and dry spells with ease, though it performs best with excellent soil drainage year-round.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Poquito Orange Agastache (Dwarf Compact Orange Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Poquito Orange is a dwarf selection bred to keep the compact scale and heavy flowering of the Poquito series in a container-friendly size.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; the dwarf, tidy habit makes this cultivar equally at home in a rock garden, mixed container, or the front edge of a sunny border. Poquito Orange stays compact while still producing a steady flush of small, tubular orange flowers over narrow, aromatic foliage from early summer into fall. Its small size does not reduce its appeal to pollinators, as hummingbirds and bees continue to visit the flower spikes throughout the long bloom season. Good drainage is essential for winter survival, since dwarf agastache selections are especially prone to crown rot in soggy soil.

common_name: Little Adder Agastache (Dwarf Compact Purple-Blue Hyssop)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Little Adder is a compact sport of the popular Black Adder agastache, retaining the dark purple-blue flower spikes on a smaller, more garden-scale plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, spacing plants closely enough to form a dense, low drift of color. Little Adder carries dense, narrow spikes of deep purple-blue flowers over aromatic, anise-scented foliage from midsummer into fall, and its compact scale suits smaller borders and containers where the larger Black Adder would be out of proportion. The tightly packed flower spikes are rich in nectar and draw bees and butterflies consistently through the bloom season, while the fine-textured foliage remains attractive even between flushes of bloom. As with other agastache, sharp drainage is critical for reliable overwintering.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Six Hills Giant Catmint (Large Lavender-Blue Perennial Catmint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, average soil in full sun; Six Hills Giant is one of the largest catmint cultivars commonly grown, forming a substantial, sprawling mound considerably bigger than Walker's Low.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, average garden soil in full sun, allowing plenty of room for the large, arching mound to spread. Six Hills Giant produces long, loose spikes of lavender-blue flowers over gray-green, aromatic foliage from late spring into summer, and shearing the plant back by about a third after the first flush encourages a strong rebloom into fall. Its large size and billowing habit make it an effective informal hedge or border filler, softening the edges of paths and mixing well with roses and ornamental grasses. The abundant flowers are highly attractive to bees and butterflies throughout the long bloom season, and established plants are notably drought-tolerant.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in evenly moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike most catmints, Nepeta subsessilis selections such as Sweet Dreams tolerate consistently moist soil and light shade without declining.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; this species tolerates more moisture and shade than the more drought-adapted Nepeta racemosa and Nepeta x faassenii cultivars. Sweet Dreams forms an upright, non-sprawling clump of broad, dark green foliage topped with dense clusters of rose-pink flowers from mid to late summer, giving it a tidier habit and a flower color distinct from the blue and lavender tones typical of most catmints. It combines well at the edge of a woodland border or in a perennial bed with part-day sun, and its late-season flowers are a valuable nectar source for bees and butterflies when many earlier-blooming perennials have finished.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Dawn to Dusk Catmint (Pink-Flowered Giant Catmint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Dawn to Dusk is a Nepeta grandiflora selection valued for its unusual soft pink flower color among catmints, most of which bloom in shades of blue or lavender.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade, and provide a bit more consistent moisture than is typical for drought-adapted catmint cultivars. Dawn to Dusk forms an upright, clumping mound of large, coarsely textured leaves topped with loose spikes of soft pink flowers from early to midsummer, standing out from the many blue- and lavender-flowered catmints in the trade. The clump-forming, non-invasive habit makes it a good choice for a mixed perennial border where a spreading catmint would be unwelcome, and the flowers attract bees and butterflies steadily through the bloom period. Cutting the plant back after the first flush can encourage additional bloom later in the season.

common_name: Cat's Pajamas Catmint (Compact Early-Blooming Dwarf Catmint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, average soil in full sun; Cat's Pajamas is a compact, densely mounding catmint bred to stay tidy without the sprawling, floppy habit common in larger catmint cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, average soil in full sun, spacing plants so the dense, rounded mounds can fill in without overlapping. Cat's Pajamas produces abundant short spikes of lavender-blue flowers over fine, gray-green aromatic foliage beginning in late spring, holding its compact, tidy form through the season far better than taller, more sprawling catmint cultivars. The dense flowering habit and small stature suit edging, rock gardens, and containers where a full-size catmint would quickly overwhelm the space. Bees visit the abundant flowers steadily through the bloom period, and shearing lightly after the first flush encourages continued flowering into summer.
